videos.title: howard green   using the integrated tennis shapes  supporting transfer of training to the court (1080p)

segments.description: Please welcome Howard Green, co-creator of Tenor Super Movers, a youth fitness program designed to support young players from 8 and under through to 18 and under on their athletic journey. Howard has been the athletic director at Bolton Arena Academy in the UK since 2009, working with both national juniors and top WTA and ATP professionals. Today he will present using the integrated tennis shapes, supporting transfer of training to the court, sharing his holistic approach to tennis specific athletic development. Welcome Howard. Hi and welcome to my presentation. Today we're going to be looking at the topic of tennis fitness with the title of using the integrated tennis shapes and we're going to be using those to support transfer of training to the court. So first of all, big thank you for taking the time to watch this presentation and also to the organizers for asking me to be a part of it. Always enjoy sharing my thoughts on training for tennis. So in terms of what we're going to cover in this talk, a little bit look at the role of strength and conditioning in preparing the tennis athlete. My specific frameworks that I use within my practice will look at what the integrated tennis shapes are. I also want to touch on some practical elements that you can help with your coaching from tomorrow using the constraints lead approach and then give you a bit of an insight and some practical

delivery from myself and some of the coaching strategies that I use with my athletes every day. So my journey and high performance started in the military. I was in the Royal Marines, joined in 2001, busy time, 9-11 happened and the reason I kind of talk about this is it really shaped me as a person but also as a coach. The way that I am in terms of being diligent and expecting a certain level of discipline from the athletes is surrounding this and from a coaching perspective, I believe in the concept of preparation and also rehearsal. How close does our rehearsal, i.e. training look like battle, i.e. match play. So it's really important that we're always tying things back to the match court. So I've been involved at Bolton Arena Tennis Academy in the near Manchester in the UK since 2009, started volunteering all the way back in 2009 and I've been a big part of the program shortly after finishing my coaching degree, got the opportunity to lead out the program, been doing that now for over a decade. At the centre we work with juniors all the way from Mini Reds all the way through to under 18s but I've also had a great opportunity to work with a number of professionals ranging from world number ones to upcoming British players such as Anna Ravanovich, Heather Watson and my young pro Marnie Banks. And also I've had an amazing opportunity to present my thoughts on training, this is actually a

pitch from back in 2018 where I presented in person at the Australian Open Coaches Conference and it's something that I enjoy very much. So in terms of strength and conditioning, I believe it has a dual role with the first one being looking to improve performance which will then lead to winning more matches and becoming harder to beat but we have this secondary role where we're looking to reduce the risk of injury which then boosts overall availability and then this is where we create the greatest opportunity for tennis players to become better and that's been on the tennis court. Yes the work we do in the gym and the plyometrics and speed work do supports it but it's then the application of those physical qualities actually in tennis practice and tennis competition is where they become better players. So if we look at this graph here on frequency and importance so there's many things that happen very frequent but don't have a great level of importance. These are average rally lengths, the average serve speed that might come up against but where S&C can help in my opinion the things that don't happen very frequently but have a high level of importance so very long rallies dealing with somebody with a huge serve, dealing with somebody who's got amazing drop shots. If we can get to that drop shot, if we can deal with that big serve, if we can outlast the opponent, these are all things in my opinion going to have

like a psychological effect and are also going to kind of swing momentum so if this play usually out serves people and nobody can deal with it but you've got the reaction speed and return skills to deal with it then that can affect your opponent. If you can last these long 20-25 shot rallies and come out on top that's going to negatively affect the momentum and mental capacity of your opponent. So I have a mentality of working from tots to toe so what we're looking at is what can we be doing with our mini red players that lay the foundation for their future success wherever that might be playing for the county or the country or becoming a professional what can we thread in from a young age develop the habits develop the skills that they'll need to succeed whatever the tennis journey may be and what I've done now is taken my experience of working with these professional players my experience of working in the military and then reversed engineers so what can we do what can we learn from that those experiences and then reverse engineer and start to lay those foundations from as young as possible. So a mission statement and my mission statement is to help my players win more matches become harder to beat and enjoy lifelong participation taking into consideration they're not everybody wants to be a professional not everybody wants to compete internationally they may just want to play tennis for the rest of their lives. So in terms of having frameworks it's

important because if we want to apply s and c principles then it's important to have systems and processes to guide that implementation so I have an overarching framework that provides themes and a more in-depth framework that actually looks at the exact session theme the content and the exercise selection. So my overarching theme has been heavily influenced by Pierre Paganini who's a Federer's trainer spent some time in Switzerland with Benny Linder and this is a framework that they use and these different elements could be the theme of the session they could be the theme of a block of training or we can link it to long-term athlete development in that younger players are going to spend more time in one end than the other so general training orientated training integrated training specific training so a young player is going to do four more general work than they are doing specific work and as they progress through their athletic and tennis playing career more specific work than general. So the objective in general training is just to build an athlete so we're going to use a variety of different fitness qualities strength endurance flexibility and agility and these are our basic skills drills exercises that work on fundamental tennis skills and footwork hand-eye coordination and basic stroke techniques so that's why and what we're going from a physical perspective and then the sort of basic stuff that the tennis coach will be working on but ultimately we're

going to be looking for a level of variety especially at a young age and encouraging continue to participate in other sports and if that's not possible in my practice we'll add multi sports into our fitness sessions whether it be working on some um hand-eye coordination with hockey or bowl skills with basketball we'll add that into our practice. Now orientated training what we're trying to do is turn that general athlete into a tennis athlete so now the exercises that we use are going to look at a lot more like tennis itself. From a gym perspective we might build the strength in general phase with squats but then in this phase we might go more to our single leg exercises for example. Integrated training this is where we combine both physical work and tennis in a way that closely simulates what match is going to look like so we'll blend a physical exercise with a tennis exercise so that might be something with myself with a med ball or banded exercise we then remove those and we go straight into some hitting so this is where the s and c coach works hand in hand with the tennis coach at the same time in the same session from tennis perspective we can also start to layer in some mental training to incorporate elements on focus and resilience so we can actually build up a level of fatigue and get them to perform under that fatigue. Our specific training looking to fine-tune these physical skills now

and from a tennis perspective looking to peak towards our heat tournaments so our drill is going to be short they're going to be intense and they're going to replicate match play. We're also having emphasis on recovering injury prevention getting them ready for those bigger tournaments. In a specific training scenario what that might look like is a basket drill but what's going to happen is the work to rest ratio will be set by the physical trainer so we're using exact tennis exercises and movements and situations but to get a physiological outcome. So as we move from that overarching framework and go to something a little bit deeper then I use my smash framework which covers strength movement agility stability and honing coordination skills and I'll go into depth a little bit more on each of these shortly. I'm then going to have a theme to my session whether that be forward and back side to side on multi-directional so for example if the tennis theme within the training block at the academy might be rally threshold then using our side to side themed exercises and sessions would be beneficial if they're working on serve volley then we might gravitate to our forward and back and if we're dealing with defending then multi-directional exercises and sessions will better match the tennis. So what I want to give now is for each of those smash components a target athletic quality and then what the positive transfer to tennis is and this is

because in my opinion context is king and if everybody involved player coach and s and c and maybe parent is clear on why we might do a certain type of physical training then in my opinion we're going to get a much better buy-in if the play is clear okay we're doing this work in the gym because it's going to impact this and then it's going to impact my performance like this so by being clear on what we're trying to do and communicating that with the player we get better buy-in better accountability and better autonomy so our strength work that we'll do ultimately is being to create strong tennis shapes on the court using general exercises to sport specific as these underpin all of our tennis movement so squat patterns lunch patterns in different directions are going to prepare them for what we need to use on the court and you'll see I'll use these yellow lines overlaying the physical exercise and then showing how that shape would then be used in a tennis specific scenario so I can use these images with my athletes to go look we're developing this lunge pattern because in closed stance back and dealing with the slides you're going to have to have a strong foundation in order to deal with that so that's why I've got to concentrate on this exercise movement here's where we work on developing fundamental movement skills so our running hopping skipping jumping etc and that's because it lays the foundation for all

athletic movement so at a younger age far more fundamental movement skills before progressing into sport specific skills so simple examples might be moving around an area using different footwork patterns and then integrating a balanced exercise such as the single leg rdl as we'll see here that will be a common shape that we'll need after serving so we can thread in and disguise this work our agility work we're looking to create our athletes have an ability to move at both speed and intensity and that's going to improve their ability to move the shots in all directions we can do close drills like this where it's just a crossover repeated action what I tend to do now with all of these movements even if it's a closed drill such as this I will add a signal so the movement will be created on a signal from my hand might be a dropping of a ball a movement of a racket face to dictate whether they move to the left or right and again we're going to within those drills have specific shapes that we're trying to work on stability is vital and we need to develop both static and dynamic balance because that's going to help us deal with shots of all different difficulty whether they're on stretch whether in zone one movement the more stable we are both dynamically and statically we can deal with those scenarios try to do a lot of drills where we kind of reinforce this wide ready position the ability

of the lower body to pivot and twist and turn just like we will need to do on the court and again they're going to have these underpinning shapes that we're trying to chase and then coordination and coordination is the definition for me that I use from John Kiley's the least uptake of resources to solve a movement puzzle or movement problem the more coordinated an athlete is the better they are dealing with different situations in a more efficient manner and also it's going to underpin your match skills so if somebody's more coordinated the skills at the net would be higher often if we're doing these sort of drills we'll combine movement with a ball if it's just a single and or a self led drill from a player and even here just looks like quite a simple drill we're still going to have these target shapes that we're disguising in there whether it's the ready position or deceleration shapes or the acceleration shapes we'd need to get to a drop shot and then we go from this overarching into a more in-depth and now specifically integrated shapes what are they ultimately what they do they provide a process and a framework to create a common lens so when we're observing we're all looking at our movement on court with a common lens if we're discussing movement on the court we're going to use a common language and then if there's an intervention required i.e a movement doesn't look like we want it to do trying to delve deep into why that is

is it because the player can't won't or doesn't know how can't they don't have the physical ability to do so we may have tightness around the hips or weakness won't a bit more of a mental block and don't know how to a skill acquisition thing do they actually not know how to solve this movement puzzle because they don't have the underlying skills so if there's an intervention required we're clear on why it is what the intervention will be whose responsibility is it and how long will it take so if it's a can issue don't have the physical strength that very much relies on me and then we're going to gravitate towards our general and orientated training if it's won't if it's a blockage in a perceived lack of physical fitness to which underpins poor mental resilience okay we can work on that if it's i don't know how to that might be a perfect time to work on integrated training where a physical exercise can work on the shape and the pattern required that then helps and stimulates the ability to do that in a specific scenario so these shapes fit into the footwork cycle which is our start our split step our movement to the ball and around the ball the actual hit itself and then the recovery footwork that we would use to recover to restart that footwork cycle so with our movement and recovery we're going to have our different types of movement patterns be it shuffle crossover runner hit we're going to be

behind the ball or on the move and our start we're looking at the split step timing technique and reactiveness are the timing it in relation to the opponent are they using the right technique either landing with two or one foot and the next and then how sharp is that the reactiveness of that so the shapes themselves number one is the readiness to move shape we've got this triangular base and level head we've got our start the shape is going to look slightly different depending on how far we need to move so the one on the left we're not moving very far we might split open the hip turn the racket whereas if we're having to chase a ball in the trams then that's going to look more like a sprint type shape with this inside leg having what we call a positive shin angle so here we're having to accelerate quicker towards the ball so therefore this shape on the right is more relevant our load and rotate shape either behind the ball or on the move are we using the ground well or we're using the kinetic chain well to set up for the best transfer into the shot if we are wide on the court then we're going to have to use the stock shape where we're having to decelerate before then setting up with that load and rotate shape and then finally the recovery shape always looking to recover at speed into the right place at the right time and ideally before the opponent hits so with better shapes with better kind of recovery shapes this

is positive shin angle again that we saw if we're accelerating towards a ball we would use to accelerate back to our recovery position when it comes to the shapes it's really what I dial into with my athletes on an education standpoint on a buying standpoint that hey these are the shapes that we see most common on the sport therefore we need to be able to create the shapes but on the flip side from a tactical standpoint if we can create and observe and recognize good shapes within our own body then we can recognize poor shapes on the other side we can see where the player is off balance where they're on full stretch and that can indicate that we're going to get an easier ball so therefore our goal then is to break the shapes of the opponent what can I do tactically to move that player around to create a poor shape that then I might get a short ball off so we've got this theme to the session the block or a long-term athlete development we've got the exercising themselves and then we thread those into the specificity of the shapes required on court the constraints led approach are also known as chocolate covered broccoli how can we disguise quality work without the player even knowing it so ultimately it's a method that we can use in coaching that shapes the athlete's environment which then drives them to improve the performance and skills and what we're going to see is manipulating different types of constraints

so that overall we can create a dynamic learning environment that promotes skill acquisition adaptable athletes and also over time enhance the player to be able to learn more autonomously so what we can do with a constraints approach is create much more realistic learning environments we can create scenarios that are similar to that that they might find in match play by manipulating different tasks we can guide the skills that we want to drive by manipulating the environment by using zones on the court asking players to hit into certain zones and moving to others this is where that we can actually guide and enhance the skill and learning we can also create individual constraints from a coaching perspective we might have a squad session but in constraints that we put on each player might be slightly differently either to further challenge exactly what they need to work on and make sure we've got this level of struggle within a session that players aren't just succeeding all the time there's that level of struggle that it takes a lot level of concentration in order to be successful which by doing these things creates athletes who are better at solving problems and can become more creative and it's also recognising that learning in general skill acquisition is not a linear approach there's going to be ups there's down there's going to be plateaus and by being creative in our coaching and the way that we set up our

drills we can keep that progression moving forward so what i've tried to do here is give you some practical delivery a fly on the wall situation and in each of these coaching situations i've got a target shape in mind i'm using a drill from the smash framework and then i'm going to use a constraints leg coaching tool and ultimately what i'm trying to do is minimal amount of coaching and use the exercises as movement puzzles to guide what i want from the player so within this first drill my target shape is the readiness to move shape the drill i'm going to use is from movement within smash and it's a sidestep drill and from a coaching strategy i'm going to use analogies by using analogies we can improve memory retention we'll find from session to session they can pick up and remember and what we've done before allows visualization if we use age and stage appropriate analogies it's easier for the player to kind of link and see it in the mind so for example when we're using sprints we talk about taking off like a jet punching the ground behind you and then we can also increase engagement by kind of using analogies that are relevant to that age group whether that might be cartoons or a player and we get better engagement of the players from that so you can see there that i've used that analogy of banging the head on the roof that then reinforces the coaching that i did so i developed the ready position the dynamic

balance position and then as we put it into more movement and then using this analogy of the roof to keep them in that wide low base so in this next drill my target shape is the load and rotate i'm going to use a stability drill called diagonal rotations and from a coaching strategy what i'm going to use is mirroring so by using mirroring what we can do is tap into those that are visual learners and we get immediate feedback as they can see what the coach is doing and therefore correct the movement patterns and we've found it's actually a much quicker way to improve technique rather than it's just basically stopping you from over coaching so if you can mirror something quickly and show them they can copy and sometimes it reduces the amount of words that we need to get the desired outcome you'll see within the video that i'll kind of point somebody out get them to look at me and then try mimic what i'm doing and what we can do is once they become competent then they can use each other to mirror and from a skill acquisition skill acquisition standpoint we can get these mirror neurons whereas if we're observing somebody else we actually get a rep of the exercise and then what we want to do over time is almost get the athletes coaching each other so if they can pick up errors if we're squatting and knees are curving in and the athlete can ask their partner to push the knees apart that's just reaffirming their learning and giving them a better and deeper

understanding of each movement pattern in our next drill we're looking to create the stop shape i'm using an acceleration to deceleration stopping a squat position from our agility drills and from a coaching standpoint i'm using a variety of signals by using signals improve responsiveness they're always reacting into a signal when they're on the court when they're performing so we can improve that cognitive flexibility they can pick up the ability to read signals from different positions from different elements so as we talked earlier they're going to start to pick up signals in the opponent's body before the ball even gets there they can see them off balance then we start to think okay this is where i'm going to get that shorter ball and we can get improved focus and attention because we're varying things up we're constantly challenging the brain as well as the body so we can see in that scenario on the first example i used an arm drop so they're just searching for a simple signal and they can respond quicker with the ball on the first rep i threw the ball up so we're asking waiting for them to time watch it come down and go so a little bit like they might observe that ready to do the split step and on the last one i threw the ball down fast so that's where that's tapping into that responsiveness are they alert are they ready in order to move quickly so we can see there we had this target set of shot of stop if we screenshot

the athletes then we can see we are developing that skill with a movement puzzle we don't talk about that stop shape explicitly but by giving them a target zone to stop in in a specific shape then we're looking for those athletes to use that solution and use that shape to fix the actual movement puzzle next we've got tight shape of start and recover i'm using a coordination drill ball throw and catch and i've got several tools that i'm using here i'm using drill layering i'm using questioning and i'm using chaos now by using layering it's a great way to progress skill we can start with a simple level and then slowly build it up that builds the confidence within the athlete okay i've been successful there next challenge next challenge and it also allows us to kind of see you as we progress through the levels if there's an error here if we'd have gone to the big open drill straight away it could be a number of things that's creating an error in the movement but by taking it step by step we can eliminate any issues as we move along really good tool to use questioning and that's going to really enhance the understanding and often players will just say yes yes i understand but actually using a bit of questioning can delve into that gets them to critically think about what's going on and then encourages a bit of self-reflection if we're encouraging them back and forth or using open questions if we want to then play do some match

play bring them off the court get them to give some feedback then they've got this skill of being a critical thinker and being able to reflect accurately on what's happened from a chaotic standpoint tennis players need to be super adaptable surface opponents situations environments we've got always looking to drive decision-making so by making these chaotic situation and responding to different things it's going to help them with that when they're in the heat of battle and then we can also really delve deep and simulate game conditions by using specific elements to create that chaos when you're ready get three go so a lot going on long video there so with the questioning in terms of chart in charge of the ball in charge of the body we'd then relate that to the court you're in charge of both of those things you're in charge of the flight path of the ball where you hit it and by yourself some time you can move quickly and recover and get into the right positions we saw initially when they were practicing just going to the court and coming back we saw a different a number of different strategies one player size stepping one using kind of a crossover and accelerating so I intervened and corrected that you could see how that drill was built up from just throwing a ball to just moving to adding those elements together so you can kind of see how all those things come together to improve the rate which the players are going to improve this and you probably picked

up on it but this guy here in the raffa top really stood out in this session as a really optimal mover naturally by presenting movement puzzles we could see that this guy moves well when he's moving towards the cone and recovering he adopted these shapes so without being explicit we've got these kind of key shapes addressed with movement puzzles so as a recap we went over what the actual role of strength conditioning is in preparing the tennis athletes I took you through a few different frameworks we looked at what the integrated tennis shapes and how they are can really become this vehicle to help transfer of training onto the court by constantly observing movement in the same way talking about it using a common language and being clear on what our interventions are what they are whose responsibility how long it's going to take and why there is an intervention required is it they can't they won't or they don't know how by using the constraint set that let approach we can use things like analogies we can use layering we can use questioning to really shape the learning environment and shape the constraints that drive us towards the shapes that we want to create without being explicit by creating chocolate covered broccoli hiding the work with drills and then what I tried to do is just give you a bit of an insight into some practical delivery with a certain age group of players and some of the coaching strategies

I would use with them in order to achieve the goals of the session so on the left if click here this is my instagram account and only a short amount of time so I couldn't share everything that I do on a daily basis but if you go to this this account you're going to see drills from eight year olds to 18 year olds to professional players using all the different elements from smash on the right if you scan that QR code you get a completely free session from the super mover program a side-to-side session that you can use with your players and then if you need to contact me ask any questions there's my email and more information on what we do at supermovers and the program that we have you just visit the website at the bottom thank you very much for listening and I'll catch you soon
